lesson.title: The Triangular Trade: Weaving Slavery into the Atlantic Economy
lesson.summary: A web of Atlantic shipping routes linked European manufactured goods, enslaved Africans, and American raw materials into an interdependent trading system that made colonial slavery economically central to England, Africa, and the Americas alike.
lesson.body:
Historians use the term triangular trade to describe the network of shipping routes that connected Europe, West Africa, and the Americas from the sixteenth through the nineteenth centuries, though in practice individual voyages rarely followed a neat three stop pattern and ships often carried varied cargoes depending on markets and seasons. Still, the basic outline captures how deeply the Atlantic economy depended on the labor system already taking hold across the Southern Colonies and beyond. On one leg, European merchants shipped manufactured goods, cloth, firearms, metal tools, and alcohol, to West African ports. On a second leg, African traders and European merchants exchanged captives for these goods, and enslaved Africans were then transported across the Atlantic in the notoriously brutal Middle Passage. On a third leg, raw materials produced by enslaved labor in the Americas, sugar, tobacco, rice, and later cotton, were shipped back to Europe.

New England colonies developed a particularly direct stake in this system despite lying far from the plantation economies of the South. Merchants in ports like Boston and Newport distilled rum from molasses imported from Caribbean sugar plantations, then shipped that rum to West Africa to trade for captives, who were carried to the Caribbean or mainland colonies and sold, with the profits often reinvested in more molasses. This pattern tied New England's economy to slavery just as surely as it tied the plantation South, even though relatively few enslaved people remained in New England itself.

The scale of the trade was immense. Historians studying shipping records estimate that more than twelve million Africans were forced aboard ships bound for the Americas over the roughly three and a half centuries of the trade, with a substantial share dying during the Middle Passage crossing due to disease, malnutrition, and the horrific conditions belowdecks. Those who survived were sold into a labor system that, as slavery hardened into a hereditary, race based institution across the colonies, offered essentially no path to freedom.

The triangular trade illustrates how thoroughly the Atlantic world's economies had become interlocked by the eighteenth century. Enslaved labor in the Americas produced the raw materials that fed European industry and consumer demand, the profits from selling those goods financed further slaving voyages to Africa, and the entire system generated enormous wealth for merchants, shipbuilders, and investors on both sides of the Atlantic. This trade did not simply supply labor to existing colonies, it actively shaped which crops colonies grew, which ports prospered, and which economic interests would come to dominate colonial politics in the decades leading up to the American Revolution.
